title: Parallel Lines Cut by a Transversal
short: Corresponding and alternate angles are equal.
trouble: Students assume angle pairs are equal even when the lines are not parallel.

blocks.html: You know vertical and supplementary angles. When a line, called a transversal, crosses two parallel lines, it makes eight angles, and they come in just two sizes.

Slide the top crossing down along the transversal (a translation). Because the two lines are parallel, it lands exactly on the bottom crossing, so each angle at the top matches the angle in the same position at the bottom: corresponding angles are equal. Add what you already know (vertical angles are equal, angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$), and all the other pairs follow.

When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, corresponding, alternate interior and alternate exterior angles are equal, and same-side interior angles add to $180^\circ$. Every angle is one of two sizes, and the two sizes add to $180^\circ$.

blocks.name: angle
blocks.cap: Turn the transversal and pick a kind of pair. The angles are numbered 1 to 4 counterclockwise at the top crossing (1 is upper right), and 5 to 8 the same way at the bottom.

blocks.title: Find the others
steps: $\angle 5$ is in the same position at the other crossing: corresponding, so $65^\circ$.
$\angle 6$ sits next to $\angle 5$ on a straight line: $180^\circ - 65^\circ = 115^\circ$.

blocks.title: With algebra
blocks.q: Two alternate interior angles measure $(3x + 10)^\circ$ and $(5x - 30)^\circ$. Find $x$ and the angles.

blocks.name: g8-transversal
blocks.cap: When the lines are not parallel, $\angle 1$ and $\angle 5$ differ. Press the button to make them parallel again.

blocks.html: Using the angle-pair rules when the lines are not parallel. The rules come from sliding one crossing onto the other, which only works for parallel lines. Look for the arrow marks (or the word “parallel”) before you use them.
